Shah Jahan was devastated. The court historians wrote: "The king cried out with grief, like an ocean raging with storm . . . For the whole week afterward, His Majesty did not appear in public . . . From constant weeping, he was forced to use glasses, and his hair turned grey." The emperor grieved for two years, and historians recorded that he never showed enthusiasm for administering his empire again. Instead, Shah Jahan found solace in art and architecture. Six months after his wife’s death, he began planning a magnificent memorial to his wife, a memorial to love. This memorial would consist of Arjumand’s tomb, ornamental gardens, and several other buildings. Set on the banks of the Jamuna River near Shah Jahan’s palace in Agra, the complex became the Taj Mahal.

At this time, the Mughal Empire was at its peak and India was an extremely wealthy country. Consequently, Shah Jahan spared no expense in planning and building the Taj Mahal. The finest artisans and craftsmen were summoned from all over Asia. The chief architect was a Persian engineer and astrologer, Ustad Ahmad. Sculptors, designers of domes, stone carvers, calligraphers, accountants, and construction supervisors came from Persia, Syria, Turkey, and India. Similarly, building and ornamental materials were sourced from all corners of Asia and the Middle East. There was jade from China, turquoise from Tibet, and amber from Myanmarㅡover forty types of gemstones in all. The main building materials were white marble and red sandstone. Twenty thousand workers and one thousand elephants worked for twenty-three years and completed the Taj Mahal in 1653.

Arjumand’s tomb is situated almost three hundred meters from the entrance gate, at the opposite end of the surrounding garden. Four tall towers, or minarets, rise from its corners, and in the middle, there is a massive white dome. The tomb is made of white marble and has eight rooms inside on two floors. The central room is octagonal and contains the remains of Empress Arjumand and Shah Jahan.

It was often said that the Taj Mahal was "built by Titans and finished by jewelers." The walls, floors, doors, and ceilings of the Taj Mahal and all its buildings are beautifully decorated. In one technique, gemstones are inlaid in the marble to make exquisite glittering patterns. In another technique, red pigment is used to create delicate floral patterns on the white walls. The Taj Mahal’s entrance gate is richly decorated with floral patterns made from gemstones and with calligraphy in black marble.

When you picture the Taj Mahal, you usually think only of the majestic, white-domed building. But in fact, everything around the tomb was designed to harmonize perfectly with it: the main gateway, the gardens, the mosque, and the rest house. A detached gateway is a feature of Muslim architecture. It is a symbol of the transition between Earth and paradise.

A long garden runs from the gate to the tomb. The garden is Persian in style, with patterns based on the Islamic holy number of four. There are two marble canals that cross in the middle and divide the garden into four squares. The canals are lined with cypress trees, which symbolize death. Each of these smaller gardens is also sub divided by pathways into four flower beds. The garden was carefully designed so that there is a clear, unobstructed view of the tomb from any place on the grounds. At the center of the garden, halfway between the tomb and the gate, there is a raised marble tank containing water and lotus flowers. The tank was designed to perfectly reflect the Taj Mahal in its water.

On either side of the tomb are red sandstone buildings; one is a mosque and the other is a rest house. Like all mosques, the mosque faces toward Mecca and is used for prayer. In front, a small piece of marble is polished so highly that it reflects like a mirror. The mosque floor sparkles with the color of red velvet and the ceiling is painted in a beautiful, hypnotic pattern. The other sandstone building is the twin of the mosque; it is identical in size and design. Because it faces away from Mecca, it has never been used for prayer. It was built as a rest house and for architectural balance, so that the tomb has two identical buildings on either side.

The architects and craftsmen who worked on the Taj Mahal used some very special optical effects to enhance its grandeur and beauty. The first effect was the use of repetition. For example, the arch of the entrance gate is shaped like the tomb, so as you enter, you anticipate seeing its form. A second effect is due to the tomb’s location. As you start walking toward it, it seems to grow in size, and the dome seems to slowly inflate. When you finally reach the base, it is colossal and magnificent. The other impressive effect is an optical illusion created by the calligraphers. Holy text from the Koran decorates many buildings, including the tomb itself. However, no matter how high the text is on a wall or ceiling, its size never seems to change! This effect was achieved by gradually increasing the height of the letters.

Finally, the designers used nature to enhance the Taj Mahal’s beauty. The sky is the background to the white marble building. Of course, this background constantly changes, and as the sky changes, the Taj Mahal changes too. At night, when the sky is dark, the Taj Mahal glistens in the moonlight. At sunset, when the sky is pink, the Taj Mahal softly glows. So, the Taj Mahal is captivating for many reasons: it is a monument to love, its architectural and artistic beauty is incomparable, and it has a spiritual quality that sets it apart from other buildings. When you see it you can’t help wondering, does it belong to Earth or heaven?

24.title: Machu Picchu: The Lost City of the Incas

paragraphs.text: Picture a scene from the Indiana Jones adventure movie trilogy: The hero, a modern adventurer and archaeologist named Indiana Jones, is in the tropical jungles of India. He fearlessly climbs a tall cliff, travels through the rain forest, dodges poison arrows, and crosses a rope bridge. Despite their extreme exhaustion and the drizzling rain, Jones and his team keep walking through the mountains. Their destination is a ridge, reported to be the location of the ancient ruins of the "Temple of Doom." The men stop to rest at a small clearing. Indiana Jones notices the rocks are unusually flat. He pulls away a vine to reveal a stone wall carved with words and pictures. All the men cheer, and Indiana cheers the loudest—at last they have found the Temple of Doom.

Is this story of Indiana Jones fact or fiction? "Fiction, of course!" would be the correct answer. But the inspiration for the daredevil explorer Indiana Jones was a real-life person, the American archaeologist and explorer Hiram Bingham. Bingham had many adventures as he explored the jungles of South America in the early twentieth century. However, Bingham’s greatest achievement was in 1911, when he made one of the most important archaeological discoveries of the century, Machu Picchu. Machu Picchu is a city in the Andes Mountains of Peru, South America. It was built by the Inca people between 1440 and 1470. It is sometimes called the Lost City of the Incas because it remained hidden in the jungle for over four hundred years. Machu Picchu is extraordinary because it is so well preserved and because it shows the exceptional skills and knowledge of the Incas.

The Incas were a tribe who lived near the city of Cuzco, Peru, in the twelfth century. From the twelfth century to the mid-sixteenth century, the Inca Empire expanded and encompassed most of South America. The Incas were able to rule this territory because their society was very regimented and productive. The Incas developed highly sophisticated agriculture, architecture, engineering, government administration, education, health care, and fabric-making technology. Incan buildings were stable and able to withstand the region’s frequent earthquakes. Temples were constructed completely without mortar; instead the stones were cut to fit together exactly. Almost five hundred years later, Incan forts and temples stand in near-perfect condition. No other civilization in the world could cut and assemble stone blocks so perfectly.

The biggest concern for the Incan government was feeding its massive empire. Growing crops was difficult in the high and rocky terrain of the Andes Mountains. However, the Incas designed farmland for corn, potatoes, and medicinal plants by shaping their hills into level strips of fertile ground. These terraces were so successful that in the fifteenth century, there was more land being cultivated in the area than there is today. Recently archaeologists set up sample crops using Incan farming methods and produced more food per acre than they could with modern methods.

Incan government and education was also highly organized. All citizens in the Inca Empire aged 13 were required to take an intelligence test. If they failed the test, they were trained in a trade, and if they passed the test, they were sent to Cuzco and became public servants. It is believed that a few of these brilliant public servants were selected to work at Machu Picchu as assistants to the royal family. A position at Machu Picchu was special; it is estimated that a maximum of only 1,200 people resided there at any one time. The Incan royal family and their guests spent time there, but most residents were workers, including potters, stonemasons, silversmiths, goldsmiths, and weavers.

Some experts believe that Machu Picchu was a summer retreat for Incan nobility and royalty because the Incan emperor at the time, Pachacuti, enjoyed its incredible natural beauty. But Machu Picchu was an attractive place for other reasons too; the weather was cool, and it was quiet and isolated. These factors made it an ideal place for recreation, reflection, and conducting business during the hot Peruvian summers.

Other people think that the site was chosen because of its high altitude and isolation. It provided the perfect location for a secure military base. The royal family could use Machu Picchu to escape from any armed conflicts occurring below in Cuzco and also observe the Peruvian landscape for any potential threats.

Machu Picchu consists of over two hundred stone buildings built in typically precise Incan fashion. In fact, the stone blocks were cut so exactly that it is impossible to slide even a credit card between them. The site features three distinct areas: the religious area, the military area, and the residential area. They are separated by a majestic square. The religious area has temples and a sundial known as the Intihuatana, or "sun-catcher," shaped out of natural rock. It was also used as an altar to worship the Incan sun god, Inti. A priest or the Incan king would give speeches next to the Intihuatana. The acoustics in the main square below are perfect, comparable to those of modern auditoriums.

Machu Picchu was inhabited for about one hundred years, but its location was so remote that few people were aware of its existence. The Spanish conquered Peru in 1532, but they never found Machu Picchu. Over the next four hundred years, only a handful of farmers lived in this isolated and forgotten place. In 1911 Machu Picchu was reintroduced to the rest of the world by Hiram Bingham.

Bingham and his team had set out from Lima, the capital of Peru, on an archaeological expedition. They were searching for Vilcabamba and Vitcos, two old Incan cities rumored to be hidden in the jungle. Bingham’s expedition traveled on foot and by mule through the Urubamba Valley and into the Urubamba Gorge. There he met local people who had heard about some old ruins nearby. They led Hiram Bingham to the ruins of Machu Picchu in November of that year.

Initially Bingham was struck by the beauty and majesty of the city: "In the variety of its charms and the power of its spell," he wrote, "I know of no place in the world which can compare with it." Bingham made several trips back to Machu Picchu and took over eleven thousand photos of the site. In 1913 the site received a significant amount of publicity after National Geographic magazine devoted its entire April 1913 issue to it. Later Bingham wrote a number of books and articles about Machu Picchu; his book Lost City of the Incas became a best seller.

Today Machu Picchu is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a popular tourist attraction. In 2003 four hundred thousand people visited Machu Picchu. Despite its remote location, it is easy for a tourist to visit. First, fly to Peru’s capital, Lima. Then, from Lima, take another short flight to the city of Cuzco in the southern part of the country. Once in Cuzco, you can hire a guide and hike to Machu Picchu along the Incan Trail. This takes about four days on foot. Alternatively you can take a short train ride to Aguas Calientes, the nearest town to Machu Picchu, and then take a twenty-minute bus ride up to the ruins. Either way you will arrive at the breathtaking Machu Picchu, a sight like nothing else you will ever experience!

The air is still. There is a creaking sound. The lid of the ancient coffin slowly opens. Everyone holds their breath. I gasp, then breathe a sigh of reliefㅡI see nothing but darkness inside the coffin. But the coffin is not empty. Someoneㅡor somethingㅡis in the coffin.

It is a mummy. It rises with a jerky movement, and I gasp again. Its face and its entire body are covered loosely in bandages. The ragged bandages are yellow with age. We are frightened, but our eyes are fixed on this incredible sight. The mummy sits up completely and slowly turns to us. It begins to mutter ancient prayers that echo through the chamber. "What’s it saying?" I ask a fellow archeologist.
"We must stay with him," my colleague answers, in a strange monotone. "We must stay with him . . . forever."

Did that scene sound familiar? It could have come from any number of horror movies: The Mummy, The Mummy’s Revenge, The Mummy’s Ghost, The Mummy’s Hand, or The Mummy’s Tomb . The mummy is a fixture in Hollywood movies, but what is the real story of the mummy? Where do mummies come from? How are they made? Is there really a mummy’s curse?

A mummy is a preserved corpse. Most mummies were made deliberately, but some mummies have been preserved accidentally due to environmental conditions. The earliest mummy dates back to 3300 BC. It is a man with red hair and is displayed in the British Museum. He was buried in the hot desert sand in Africa. The hot, dry weather dried the body and prevented the flesh from decaying.

By 3030 BC, it was common practice in ancient Egypt to mummify the dead bodies of kings, queens, and the nobility. This practice continued for over three thousand years and produced over seventy million mummies. Ancient Egypt is not the only civilization to preserve its dead. Ancient cultures in Peru and Siberia also practiced mummification.

People in these cultures preserved the bodies of the dead because they believed in life after death. They believed that a person’s body must retain its physical appearance after death. The best way to do this was to preserve the body by mummification. In ancient Egypt, the mummification process took seventy days and was done by special priests who performed prayers at different stages in the process. These priests needed a detailed knowledge of human anatomy.

The first step in mummification was removing all parts of the body that would decay quickly. First, a hook was stuck up the deceased person’s nose and the brain was pulled out. This was a delicate procedure because the face could easily be disfigured. The priest then removed the internal organs, leaving only the heart, which was believed to be the center of intelligence.

The organs were preserved separately. The stomach, liver, lungs, and intestines were placed in special jars called canopic jars, which were later buried with the mummy. Next, the priests used a kind of salt called natron to dry out the body. All moisture was removed and the result was a very dried-out but recognizable human form.

The next part in the process was to fill the sunken areas of the body with linen and add false eyes. Then, the body was covered in oil, spices, and perfume and wrapped in linen bandages coated with resin. Each mummy needed hundreds of yards of linen. The priests carefully wound long strips of linen around the body, sometimes even wrapping each finger and toe separately before wrapping the entire hand or foot.

Charms were placed among the linen strips, and prayers were written on some strips for protection. At several stages, the body was coated with warm resin, and the wrapping resumed once again. When the wrapping was finished, the priests covered the body with a shroud. The mummy was complete.

People have been interested in mummies for thousands of years, although their reasons have varied. Soon after the pharaohs were mummified and buried, thieves became very interested in their mummies because they were buried in tombs filled with golden treasures. Tomb robbing became so common that the mummies were moved to secret burial places, where some remained undisturbed for thousands of years.

In the Middle Ages, it was believed that certain body parts of the mummies had medicinal properties, and so they were ground up into "mummy powder" for use in potions. In 1798, Napoleon invaded Egypt and took scientists with him to record Egyptian culture and religion. The research of these scientists was later published in Europe and included their investigation of Egyptian mummies. "Egyptology," or the study of ancient Egypt, became very popular among the upper classes.

European aristocrats became fond of collecting mummies; they would even hold special parties at which a mummy would be unwrapped. Many nobles funded or led archeological expeditions to Egypt. However, most of the ancient tombs they explored had already been disturbed or robbed. In 1891, a young Englishman named Howard Carter arrived in Egypt and trained for many years as an archeologist.

Carter was convinced that there was at least one undiscovered tomb. Under the patronage of Lord Carnarvon, a wealthy English aristocrat, Carter searched for tombs. In 1922, Lord Carnarvon summoned him to England to tell him the funding for his research had run out, but Carter convinced Lord Carnarvon to fund one final expedition. On November 4, 1922, Carter’s team discovered an ancient doorway that was still sealed. On the doorway was the name "Tutankhamun".

Upon discovering the untouched tomb, Howard Carter told Lord Carnarvon to come to Egypt immediately. When the tomb door was opened, there were many celebrations. They found the tomb undisturbed, and inside were many treasures, including the mummy of Pharaoh Tutankhamun and three gold coffins nested inside each other. There were rumors that Carter also found a tablet inscribed with a curse but immediately hid it from his workers.

A number of mysterious deaths followed, and it was thought that Tutankhamun’s mummy had cursed those who had disturbed his tomb. First, Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo of pneumonia. This created a media frenzy. News of the mummy’s curse circulated around the world. Legend has it, that by 1929, eleven of the people connected with the discovery of the tomb had died, including two of Lord Carnarvon’s relatives, and Carter’s personal secretary, Richard Bethell.

The bodies of the dead pharaohs, queens, and nobility of ancient Egypt weren’t the only things to be mummifiedㅡthe ancient Egyptians also mummified animals! Some cults in ancient Egypt worshipped animals, like the cat goddess Bast. Thousands of cats were mummified for sale to pilgrims, who presented them as offerings to the cat goddess. Vast cemeteries have been discovered containing thousands of buried cats. It is likely that cats were bred especially to be sacrificed to the Egyptian cat goddess. The Egyptians believed that their gods could become certain animalsㅡcats, hawks, crocodiles, and bullsㅡand these animals were protected, worshipped, and mummified at death. Much of our knowledge of Egyptian mummification comes from one historian in particular: Herodotus. Herodotus was an ancient Greek who observed and recorded how bodies were mummified on his travels through Egypt in 450 BC.

Mummification was practiced for over three thousand years. In 30 BC, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire. The Roman presence in ancient Egypt eventually led to the decline of the practice of mummification and the replacement of ancient religions with Christianity.

Nowadays, the technology of x-rays and computers allows us to examine mummies without unwrapping them. Their bones can be scanned and studied. DNA samples can be extracted and analyzed. Although dead for thousands of years, the mummies continue to speak to us.

26.title: Faster, Higher, StrongerㅡThe Modern Olympic Games

paragraphs.text: The Olympic Games are a sporting event like no other. They are the world’s largest sporting eventㅡthe Games have more athletes, more sports and more participant countries than any other sports competition in the world. In 2004, the Olympic Games are returning to their ancient birthplace in Greece.

The Athens Olympic Games will be held from the 13th to the 29th of August 2004. The competition schedule includes 28 Olympics sports at 35 venues. While the ancient Olympics have a long history of over one thousand years, the modern Olympics have a much shorter history.

In 1894, a French aristocrat named Pierre de Coubertin dreamt of reviving them. Like the Ancient Greeks, he believed sport had an essential role in the education system, and in the formation of strong moral character. He was also a keen sportsman himself, and practiced the sports of boxing, fencing, horse-riding and rowing.

Coubertin decided the best way to promote sport was to revive the Olympic Games. He formed an International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose job it was to organize the first modern Olympic Games. They did this successfully and in 1896, the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece. They were held in Athens as a reminder that the Olympic Games originated in Greece.

The Olympic Games in 1896 featured many references to the ancient Games. The majority of the competitions took place in the ancient stadium, which was restored for the occasion. Some of the sports from the ancient Games were echoed in the modern games, including weightlifting, wrestling and athletics. There was also cycling, fencing, gymnastics, swimming, tennis and shooting. The organizers even went as far as inventing a new race, inspired by a legendary event in Ancient Greek history: the marathon race.

This race commemorates the exploit of a soldier who, in 490 BC, ran from the town of Marathon to Athens to announce that the Persians had been defeated in battle. Legend has it that the soldier delivered the message "Niki!" ("victory"), then collapsed and died.The distance was approximately 42 km.

The modern Olympic Games have twenty-eight different sports. The IOC sets the program and decides which sports will be included. Unlike the ancient Games, individuals represent their country, and team sports like rowing, softball, baseball, basketball, soccer, volleyball and hockey are included. Until 1992, lesser known sports were also included as "demonstration sports" alongside the official Olympic program. Some demonstration sports include bandy (soccer on ice), dogsled racing and water skiing.

The Olympic program has come a long way since 1896: some sports have been discontinued (e.g. golf, polo and tug-of-war), others were dropped and then reintroduced (e.g. archery), while several new sports have been added (e.g. the triathlon and taekwondo).

For both Coubertin and the ancient Greeks, the Olympics were not just about sport. He believed this sports competition was different because it had principles: to strive for perfection, to represent the best athletes in the world and for everyone involved to display high moral character and a spirit of fair play. The symbols of the Olympic Games reflect the ideals of Coubertin and the Olympic movement. The most important Olympic symbols are the rings, the motto and the flame.

The rings represent five continents. They are interlaced to show the meeting of the athletes of the whole world during the Olympic Games. On the Olympic flag, the rings appear on a white background. The six colors of the flag, including the white background, represent all nations.

The motto is made up of three Latin words: Citius, Altius, Fortius (Faster, Higher, Stronger). These three words encourage the athlete to give his or her best during competition, and to view this effort as a victory in itself.

In memory of the Olympic Games’ origins, a flame is lit in Olympia, Greece, some months before the opening of the Games. The Olympic flame can only be lit by the sun’s rays. The flame, burning in the Olympic torch, is carried from Olympia to the host country. Past and present Olympic athletes, as well as ordinary citizens, run with the torch through towns and cities.

Modern Olympians are as legendary as the ancient Greek heroes before them. As Anita L. DeFrantz, a former Olympian, says, "Excellence comes in every shape, size, race and sex . . . Each sport takes a special skill and determination for a person to ascend to the top." Soonyung Kim was only 17 years old when she won gold medals in both the individual and team archery events at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. In the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, Kim won the silver medal in the individual event and another gold medal in the team event. She then retired at the age of 21.

Over the next seven years, Kim married and raised two children. In 1999, she started training again and qualified for the South Korean Olympic team for the Sydney Games. In Sydney, she finished third in the individual archery event. Soonyung Kim now had a complete set of medalsㅡgold, silver and bronze.

One of Korea’s most determined Olympic heroes was Keechung Sohn. As Korea was occupied by Japanese forces, Sohn had to participate in the 1936 Berlin Olympics as a Japanese team member. He was forced to use a Japanese name, Kitei Son. At the Games, Sohn resisted the pressure from the Japanese. He always signed with his Korean name, and whenever he was asked where he was from, he explained that Korea was a separate country.

Sohn became a Korean national hero when he won the Berlin Olympic marathon by more than two minutes. One newspaper, Dong-a-Ilbo , published a photo of Sohn on the victory platform-but with one change: they painted over the Japanese flag on his sweatshirt. Staff members were jailed and the newspaper’s publication was suspended. Sohn carried the South Korean flag in the Opening Ceremony of the London Olympics. Forty years later, Keechung Sohn entered the Seoul Olympic Stadium bearing the Olympic torch. The 76-year-old Sohn ran with pride and the crowd cheered him on.

Like the ancient Olympics, the modern Olympics have been the place for politics as well as sports events. In 1968 in the Mexico City Olympics, American athletes Tommy Smith and John Carlos demonstrated against racial segregation in the United States. When the American flag was raised to celebrate their victory, the athletes raised their fists and bowed their heads. This gesture showed their support for the rights of African Americans. As a result, however, they were sent home. In 1972, Palestinian terrorists took Israeli athletes hostage. They wanted to bring the world’s attention to Palestine’s situation, and demand the release of Arab hostages held by the Israelis. The event ended in tragedy when the hostages were executed by the terrorists, before in turn they were killed by the police.

At the opening ceremony of the 2000 games in Sydney, Australia, South Korea and North Korea marched together under a single flag. They were greeted by thunderous applause and tears. When the founder of the modern Olympic Games was asked, "Why did you restore the Olympic Games?" Pierre de Coubertin replied, "To ennoble and strengthen sports and to ensure their independence and duration . . ."

The 2004 Athens Olympics starts soon. During this time, athletes and spectators alike will experience some intense moments: a new record, dignity in defeat and victory, and the feeling of being part of another Olympiad.

Three thousand years ago, the ancient Greeks introduced a new sports competition. There were many athletic contests in ancient Greece, but this one was different. For a start, this competition honored the mighty Zeus, ruler of all Greek gods, so it included not only sports, but religious celebration as well. For the next thousand years, it attracted the best athletes from Greek city-states, from places as far away as modern-day Ukraine, Egypt, and Turkey.

The first of these contests took place in the Elis region of Greece, at a sacred spot called Olympia, in 776 BC. The competition was so successful that the Greeks continued to hold similar events every four years. They called these competitions the Olympic Games. So why were the Games so special?

Exercise was very important in the ancient Greek world. The Greeks believed in a well-rounded education, emphasizing exercise for the body as well as the mind. Moreover they believed that men should stay in shape in case they had to serve in the army. To promote health, every Greek city had a gymnasium and a wrestling school called a palaestra. These places were so important to each community that they also became social centers, where citizens could meet to discuss politics or listen to educational lectures.

The Olympics celebrated the importance of fitness in Greek society by providing a forum for the best athletes to come together and flaunt their skills. These people proudly represented their local communities. If someone from Athens, for example, won an event, he brought honor to his entire city-state.

The Olympic Games also had some political benefits for the Greeks. In the months before the Games started, messengers went from city to city announcing the dates of the event and that the Olympic Truce was to begin. The Olympic Truce stated that anyone involved in the Games must be allowed safe passage to Olympia, even through hostile enemy territory. The Olympic Games brought together residents of numerous city-states, allowing them to discuss politics, make alliances, and even negotiate peace.

Meanwhile athletes were training hard for the upcoming games with their coaches. Each city selected its best athletes to travel to Elis one month ahead of the Games to train on site, where they stayed in huge tents. During this period Olympic officials, who chose which athletes qualified to compete, evaluated all hopeful contestants. Those selected competed individually, not as part of a team, and competition was limited to Greek men.

Slaves, foreigners, and unmarried women could only participate as spectators. They joined the thousands of Greek men who traveled from far away to see the Games. As many as fifty thousand spectators and merchants attended the Games, camping outside under the stars. Married women, however, were prohibited from viewing the Games. If one was caught on the grounds, she was thrown off a nearby mountain as punishment!

The Olympic Festival began with an opening ceremony in a temple. This rite included the sacrifice of one hundred heads of cattle to honor Zeus. Afterwards poets and playwrights presented their works, the crowds cheered, and the Games began.

All events took place either in the stadium or the hippodrome, a track for racing horses. The very first Olympic Games lasted only three days, but by the fifth century BC, they had been extended to five days. The spectators sat on the ground, while officials watched from tents. At first the main event was a footrace, but over time more competitions were added, such as boxing, wrestling, and chariot racing.

The events back then were a little different from their modern counterparts. Boxing, for example, had no rule against hitting an opponent while he was down. The footrace sometimes became so violent that the athletes were forced to wear helmets and carry shields. Another modern development is uniforms; in the ancient Olympics, athletes competed totally nude. They did this because the Greeks had a deep appreciation for the human body and believed that displaying it was a tribute to Zeus.

Another difference between the ancient and modern Olympics is that there was only one winner in each eventㅡthere was no second or third place─and he received an olive branch as his prize instead of a medal. This may not seem like much, but a victorious athlete could live off his achievements for the rest of his life. His hometown might reward him with food, cash, honorary appointments, or leadership positions in the community. Greek writers, poets, and sculptors also recorded his story, so that his victory was never forgotten.

One such athlete was the boxer Melankomas of Caria, a town in modern Turkey. He won the boxing event in 49 AD. He was famous not only for his magnificent body and good looks, but also for his unusual fighting technique. Melankomas did not strike his opponents; rather, he wore them out by skillfully dodging their blows. It was said that he could fight all day long without tiring, even in the Greek heat.

Another legendary athlete of the ancient world was Milo of Kroton, who was from what is now Italy. He won the wrestling event at six Olympic Games between 540 BC and 516 BC. Milo enjoyed showing off his unrivaled strength and control. He would hold a piece of fruit in his hand and challenge people to take it away from him. Even though he held the fruit so tightly that no one could take it, he never damaged it. Another of his favorite tricks was to tie a string around his head, hold his breath, and break the string with the veins bulging out of his forehead!

Theagenes of Thasos became famous at the age of nine. One day, as he was walking home from school, he noticed a bronze statue of a god in the marketplace. For some inexplicable reason, Theagenes broke the statue off its base. The story of a young boy who could break bronze with his bare hands was talked about everywhere. When he was older, Theagenes competed in the Olympics and easily won the boxing prize.

Other athletes were remembered for less honorable reasons. Even though all contestants in the Games took an oath to Zeus that they would abide by the rules, some did not keep this promise. One infamous cheater was Eupolus of Thessaly, who bribed other boxers in the 98th Olympics. In the 112th Olympics, Callippus of Athens gave money to all the other athletes in his race to let him win. Cheating was punished; dishonest athletes had to pay huge fines. With this money, statues of Zeus were erected along the road that led to the stadium, with the names of the cheats inscribed on their bases. To get to the stadium, the athletes had to walk past all the statues, which reminded them of what not to do.

The Olympic Games were so important in the ancient Greek world that time was not measured in years, but in Olympiads. One Olympiad is the amount of time between each Olympic Game, four years. Things changed, however, in 146 BC, when the Romans conquered Greece. They did not worship Zeus, the Romans were Christian. In 393 AD Roman Emperor Theodosius I abolished the Olympic Games because they did not want their citizens celebrating a pagan god.

It wasn’t until the late nineteenth century that people started to think again about organizing an international sporting event and reinvented the Olympic Games. Today, almost two thousand years after the original Games ended, athletes from most countries in the world participate in the modern Olympics, a tribute to the lasting influence of the Ancient Greek heroes, their traditions, and eternal spirit.
